rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence and maximum uncertainty across all design axes (modality, encoder, profile, aggregation, fusion). The most informative first experiment is the simplest possible baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (n=2000). This establishes a clear performance floor with the least number of learned or architectural parameters (PCA is a fixed linear projection, no image branch, no aggregation, no fusion). It isolates the raw RNA signal quality and gives a reference against which every subsequent experiment—adding an image modality, switching to scVI/scGPT, enabling multiprofile with aggregation, or introducing fusion—can be directly compared. Choosing this minimal baseline first avoids confounding: if later multimodal or multiprofile configurations outperform it, we can attribute the gain to the added complexity rather than to an untested encoder choice. It is the best use of the first budget slot because it maximizes the interpretability of all future comparisons.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, PCA, singleprofile → 48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) provides a clean, single-variable test: it holds profile setting constant (singleprofile) and swaps the modality from RNA to image, using a standard pretrained encoder. If image features yield substantially higher accuracy, it strongly motivates exploring the multimodal branch (configs 016–051) and justifies budget there. If image features perform comparably or worse, it indicates the bottleneck is representation quality within a single modality, redirecting budget toward better RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the single highest-level design decision (modality contribution) before committing budget to more complex fusion/aggregation choices.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while config_010 (image, resnet50, singleprofile) achieves only 20.8%, a ~28-point gap. This leaves major uncertainty about whether the image modality is fundamentally uninformative or simply poorly encoded by resnet50. Question: config_013 swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a larger, ViT-based architecture), keeping everything else identical to config_010. This isolates the effect of image representation quality. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in multimodal fusion (configs 016-051) or multiprofile/aggregation strategies, we need to know whether the image modality can be made competitive. If imagenet_vit_l substantially closes the gap, multimodal experiments become high-value and we should prioritize them. If it does not, we can deprioritize image and multimodal paths and focus budget on RNA encoder improvements (scvi_n200, scgpt) and multiprofile aggregation. This single-variable change maximally reduces strategic uncertainty with one experiment.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 acc, far exceeding both image-only baselines (~0.21-0.23), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA) in one profile setting, leaving it unclear whether the 0.485 ceiling is due to the linear PCA representation or is inherent to the RNA signal. Question: config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_001, isolating the effect of the RNA encoder (learned nonlinear latent representation vs. linear PCA) while holding profile setting constant. Why this is best: The encoder choice is the most fundamental design decision—it will influence every downstream multimodal and multiprofile experiment. If scvi_n200 substantially outperforms PCA, it signals that learned representations are critical and justifies investing in scgpt and multimodal variants with better encoders. If it performs similarly or worse, it confirms PCA is sufficient and redirects the search toward profile/aggregation/fusion. This single experiment reduces the most consequential uncertainty with minimal confounding, making it the highest-information next step under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.485–0.520) dominate image-only models (0.208–0.227) by a wide margin, and scvi_n200 (0.520) outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485) by ~3.5 acc points. All completed experiments use singleprofile; the multiprofile axis is entirely unexplored. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) improve on the best singleprofile RNA configuration (config_004, scvi_n200, 0.520)? Why this is the best next step: config_005 changes exactly one variable (singleprofile→multiprofile with avgpool) from the current best configuration, isolating the profile-setting effect while holding the RNA encoder at its proven-best value. If multiprofile+avgpool helps, a follow-up can test transformer aggregation; if it does not, we avoid spending budget on more complex aggregation schemes. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk experiment given the current evidence.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large jump over config_004 (singleprofile, scvi_n200, 0.520), confirming multiprofile + scvi_n200 as the strongest direction. However, only avgpool aggregation has been tested; transformer aggregation is unexplored. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool for combining multiple RNA profiles with the scvi_n200 encoder? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only aggregation changes from config_005), isolating the effect of aggregation strategy. Why best next: (1) It directly extends the current best configuration along the most important untested design axis within the proven RNA-multiprofile regime. (2) The aggregation choice will propagate to all future multimodal experiments, so resolving it now reduces uncertainty for the entire remaining search. (3) It avoids the risk of simultaneously introducing image modality (which is currently very weak at ~0.21-0.23) and fusion, which would confound interpretation. (4) It is a high-information experiment: if transformer >> avgpool, we gain a clear upgrade path; if they are similar, we confirm avgpool sufficiency and can confidently move to multimodal with avgpool.

Evidence: Multiprofile with scvi_n200 yields the best results (0.650-0.653), a large jump over singleprofile scvi (0.520) and singleprofile pca (0.485). Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) is negligible (~0.3%). Uncertainty: We do not know whether the multiprofile gain is a general property of multi-view profiling or is specifically enabled by the learned scvi representation. This experiment (pca_n2000 + multiprofile + avgpool) directly isolates the encoder effect in the multiprofile regime by holding profile setting and aggregation fixed while swapping scvi→pca. If pca+multiprofile approaches 0.65, the encoder is secondary and simpler pipelines suffice; if it drops substantially, learned encoders are essential for multiprofile to work. This is the highest-information single comparison available: it clarifies the encoder×profile interaction in the performance-critical regime before investing budget in multimodal or scgpt variants that build on an untested assumption about which encoder to use.

Evidence: The best-performing configuration so far is config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, with config_006 (transformer aggregation) essentially matching it at 0.653. Image-only models are very weak (0.208–0.227), and the scvi_n200 encoder clearly outperforms pca_n2000 in both single- and multi-profile settings. However, the scgpt encoder has not been tested at all, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of which RNA representation is best. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005—the only difference is the RNA encoder (scgpt vs. scvi_n200), while profile setting and aggregation are held at their best-known values. This directly tests whether scgpt is competitive with or superior to scvi_n200 in the multiprofile regime where gains are largest. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It resolves a major uncertainty about encoder choice before committing budget to multimodal or further aggregation experiments, since the encoder decision will affect all downstream multimodal configurations. (2) It follows the principle of isolating one variable: only the encoder changes relative to the current best. (3) If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new promising branch; if it falls well short, we can confidently rule it out and focus remaining budget on multimodal fusion with scvi_n200. (4) Given that avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly equivalent for scvi_n200, using avgpool here avoids confounding the encoder question with the aggregation choice.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (best: config_006, scvi_n200/multiprofile/transformer at 0.653), while image-only models are very weak (~0.21-0.23), suggesting image features carry little standalone signal. The key remaining uncertainty is whether the image modality provides any complementary information when fused with the strong RNA representation. This experiment (config_039) directly tests that question by combining the best-known RNA setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) with the best image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) using weighted fusion, which is appropriate given the large modality strength imbalance. If it exceeds 0.653, multimodal fusion is worthwhile and we can explore fusion strategies; if it does not, we can confidently focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinement. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the central design question (is multimodality useful here?) with the strongest available components, rather than testing a weaker combination that would be harder to interpret.

The best result so far is config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted fusion, acc=0.7250), which shows a substantial ~7-point gain over the best RNA-only multi-profile model (0.6530). However, we have no direct comparison of fusion strategy in the multimodal setting. Config_038 is identical to config_039 except it uses concat instead of weighted fusion, isolating exactly one variable. This tells us whether the multimodal gain requires learned cross-modal weighting or whether a simple concatenation suffices. Understanding this is critical: if concat performs comparably, the design space simplifies considerably; if weighted fusion is clearly superior, it indicates the two modalities contribute non-uniformly and the interaction is informative. Under a limited budget, this single-variable A/B test against the current best configuration is the highest-information-per-experiment choice, directly informing whether to invest further in fusion complexity or shift attention to other design axes (e.g., image encoder choice).
